title: The Four Great Works of Sin and the Separation of Light from Darkness
arc: The teaching names four great works by which Sin organizes the men of the cosmos against one another — gluttony, fornication, greed, and war — and then sets against this fourfold proprium the single saving work of the Apostle: the separation of Light from Darkness received by faith, which exalts the one who hears it above all such men.
reading:
This chapter is built as a contrast between two opposed orderings of human life. On one side stands a fourfold catalogue of "great matters" (ⲛⲁⲃ ⲛϩⲱⲃ) that the men of the cosmos pursue with one another; on the other stands the single revealed work which the Apostle has brought — the separation of Light from Darkness. The whole arc moves from the diagnosis of the proprium's complete outward expression to the announcement of the one truth that lifts the soul out of it.

The four great works are read correspondentially as the complete external articulation of self-love through the body and its appetites. Though the title transmits "five," the surviving Coptic counts four (ⲡⲓⲩⲧⲁⲩ ⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲃ ⲛϩⲱⲃ), the number of ordered fullness in extension: the proprium displayed in every direction of natural life. The first work is set "of the mouth, that they shall eat … of their body" — the lust of appetite, self-love expressing itself through the gate of taste and consuming the natural form for its own pleasure. The second is fornication, the disordered conjunction of bodies "joining themselves into it with one another," self-love active through the generative degree, a mockery of the true conjunction figured by Mother of Life. The third is wealth, "the wealth which they desire," in which men "boast among themselves" — self-love rising into a false glory, the corrupt counterpart of celestial good (gold turned into love-of-self), the proprium reaching for honor through possession. The fourth is "the war and the [outburst] of frenzy and the injustices which they take with one another, one prevailing over another … in tyranny, that they may take a name in the world of all men." This is self-love in its dominating principle, the lion-aspect of the King of Darkness — the will to rule and to be named great, which is the inmost root of the other three made externally violent.

These four are therefore not unrelated vices but the discrete extension of a single love. They begin in the mouth (the lowest gate, mere appetite), rise into the flesh (fornication), pass into the proprium's possession (wealth and boasting), and culminate in dominion over others (war and tyranny). Together they describe the whole "body" of the King of Darkness expressed in the human community: the cosmos as the arena in which self-love uses every natural faculty to consume, mingle, possess, and rule. The teaching is precise that this dynamic is mutual — "one prevailing over another," "they slaughter one another, that they may take from them" — for self-love can produce only the war of each against each. Those who pursue these four matters end by destroying one another; the very fullness of the proprium's expression is its self-consuming.

Against this whole structure the teaching sets a single counter-movement. The one who receives "a faith and a thanksgiving" toward the Apostle, "with this likeness which I have brought," is brought into a different order entirely. The likeness brought by the Apostle is named in the next breath: "the separation of the Light from the Darkness, the Beautiful from the Bad." This is the saving work in its essence — the discriminative act of regeneration (ⲡⲱⲣⲭ), the undoing of the mingled state in which the four great works hold the soul. Where Sin mingles bodies, possessions, and dominions in mutual slaughter, the Apostle reveals the icon by which Light is distinguished from Darkness and the Beautiful from the Bad, and thereby establishes the soul in the only-begottenness and the godhead. The "obedience" with which the passage closes is the Hearing answering the Call: the faculty of the ear receiving what the Apostle's mouth has brought.

The closing judgment — "that one is exalted far more than [all other] men" — completes the arc. The four works lower men into the slaughtering cosmos where each takes a name by tyranny; the one truth received by faith lifts the receptive soul above that whole order. The teaching's spiritual logic is therefore simple and exact: the proprium, displayed in its complete fourfold extension, can produce only mutual destruction; the separation of Light from Darkness, received as faith and obedience, is the one act that breaks the cycle and exalts the soul out of the cosmos of mingled men into the order of the Father.
